newsitem.title: UK: British industry fears Euroscepticism in politics.
newsitem.headline: British industry fears Euroscepticism in politics.

text.p: UK industry leaders are worried about Euroscepticism across the political spectrum and remain totally committed to the European single market, Confederation of British Industry president Colin Marshall said on Tuesday.

"We detect Euroscepticism on both sides of the political divide and we are particularly concerned at the new political party which is strongly opposed to Europe," Marshall, who is also chairman of British Airways Plc, told BBC radio.
He was referring to the anti-European Referendum Party formed by Sir James Goldsmith to fight at elections which are expected to be held on May 1.
David Davies, Foreign Office minister for European affairs said there was no chance of Britain pulling out of the European Union.

"The government has no intention of leaving," he told BBC radio. "We agree the single market is massively important. We have made very clear the advantages of the single market, indeed we gain the most from them."
But Labour's employment spokesman Stephen Byers said the letter was a telling blow to the ruling Conservatives. "The warning by business leaders...directly repudiates the Tory line," he said.
"The government's scare tactics over Europe have backfired spectacularly. Voters want a sensible approach to Europe and Labour would deliver."
Opinion polls put Labour about 20 points ahead of the Conservatives, making them hot favourites to win the looming election.
Both parties have their fair share of Eurosceptics but of Prime Minister John Major's front-line ministers, only two are now obviously in favour of closer European integration.

Marshall said it was vital that the business voice was heard in the run-up to the election. "We want to make sure the views of business and industry are made as clear as possible about the absolute importance about remaining within that single market irrespective of the final outcome on the single currency."

European economic and monetary union is scheduled to start on January 1, 1999 but Britain has an opt-out. Officially, both the ruling Conservative and opposition Labour Party are keeping their options open on joining.
Marshall and 22 other business leaders wrote an open letter to the Financial Times newspaper on Tuesday, expressing their dismay at hostility to the European Union.
About 60 percent of Britain's trade is with EU countries.
The letter said if Britain's commitment to Europe was put in doubt it's ability to influence the forthcoming EU intergovernmental conference on the move toward EMU would be "seriously compromised."
Marshall said he was worried that the situation would get worse and the debate more hysterical the closer the election gets.

Other signatories of the letter to the FT included Unilever Plc chairman Niall Fitzgerald, British Telecommunications Plc's chief executive Sir Peter Bonfield and British Petroleum chairman Sir David Simon.
